title: I ported a 2001 C++ RTS to the browser in ~3 months. I still have the Cursor DB - 1,026 sessions, 17k model replies, and the model lineup rotated three times mid-project.
author: AnyWriting3715
selftext:
Cossacks: European Wars (GSC Game World, 2001) is the RTS I grew up on - thousands of units, formations, an economy that punishes you the second you forget about food. Last October I started porting it to the browser. Tutorial plus free play are live: [https://cossacks.b-cdn.net/dist/index.html?v=2](https://cossacks.b-cdn.net/dist/index.html?v=2) (desktop, give it a moment to load).  
  
This isn't a "vibe-coded a game" post. This is a port of an existing C++ codebase, which turns out to be a very different problem.

**What the source actually looks like**  
253 files, 192,681 lines of C++. Interface.cpp is 16,883 lines. NewMon.cpp is 16,629. Median function length is a reasonable 15 lines - but 105 functions are over 200 lines, 29 are over 500, and two are 2,517 lines each.

That last number is the whole story. In October 2025 the models I had ran a 200k context window. NewMon.cpp alone is roughly 145k tokens. One file, and there's nothing left for your question, the target code, or the answer. The full source is around 1.3M tokens.

So "paste the file and ask" was never on the table. Neither was "extract this function" - a 2,517-line Cossacks function isn't long because it's repetitive, it's long because it's a stateful monster where line 2,400 depends on a flag set at line 80.

**A concrete example**  
NewMonster::CreateFromFile - 2,517 lines, parses every unit definition in the game. In my port it's MonsterLoader.ts at 140 lines plus commandHandlers.ts at 2,553 lines. Same volume, completely different shape: one giant switch became a dispatch table. That was the pattern for the whole port - the AI was decent at recognizing the shape once I'd fed it enough of the function, and useless at holding all 2,517 lines at once.  


**Pathfinding: where I stopped trying to be clever**  
Cossacks doesn't use plain A\*. It uses a motion-field / lock-bars system, and that's precisely why hundreds of units move as a mass instead of deadlocking. I ported that approach instead of replacing it, because every modern alternative I tried looked wrong the instant a formation hit a chokepoint. The old engine's weird solution was weird for a reason.

**The model lineup changed under me three times - in three months**  
I still had the Cursor database, so these are real counts, not vibes. 1,026 sessions, \~17,200 model replies, 88 active days out of 99 calendar days:

* Oct 2025 (47% of all replies) - Claude Sonnet 4.5 (42%), GPT-5 (30%). Sonnet did the bulk translation volume; GPT-5 got the nastiest reverse-engineering questions. 
* Nov (33%) - Sonnet 4.5 + Sonnet thinking (45%), GPT-5.1, and Cursor's composer-1 for the mechanical passes.
* Dec (17%) - everything flipped: Claude Opus 4.5 (44%) and GPT-5.2 (39%). This is when the big refactors landed - the AI army, the brigade system, the city logic. They were tractable in December in a way they simply weren't in October.
* Jan 2026 - a 3% tail of cleanup on GPT-5.2-high and Opus 4.5.

Across the whole project Sonnet 4.5 was the single most-used model (\~5,000 replies), GPT-5 second (\~2,700).

The uncomfortable takeaway: the difficulty of this project dropped measurably every six weeks, for reasons that had nothing to do with me getting better at it. The refactors I gave up on in October went through in December on the first try.

Result: TypeScript + PixiJS 8, 805 files, 155,857 lines. Custom .GP asset reader (proprietary palette-indexed container) feeding packed atlases, with a Real-ESRGAN pass so 2001 textures survive modern resolutions. Custom ECS.

comments.author: Altruistic-Earth-666
comments.body: very cool, are the enemies supposed to flicker tho?

replies.author: AnyWriting3715
replies.body: Nope, not intentional - it's the tradeoff of running this in a browser tab. The original art is a few hundred MB of sprite archives, far too much to preload, so frames stream in on demand and get evicted from a texture cache under pressure. When an enemy's frame isn't cached yet it gets skipped for a beat, and enemy sprites are the colder set so they're first out. Tuning the cache helps, but some version of this is hard to avoid at that asset size

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: Having AI write a post up filled with a slew of AI-isms, including obvious and easily fixable ones like em-dashes every two sentences... does not speak well for the project and reads as low effort if you couldn't take 5 minutes to write up your own post. AI use in game dev is encouraged here, but I'm not so sure that mindset applies as universally to the human to human communication in this sub, if what I've seen in other threads is any indication. Just some food for thought, because if you did spend that much time on the project itself, it would be a shame to have it framed poorly by the post itself.

replies.author: AnyWriting3715
replies.body: Fair enough. English isn't my first language, so I had AI do the write-up while I focused on the actual port. Point taken though, next one I'll write myself even if it comes out rougher.

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body:
And what rules did you implement for the refactoring? 
Did the ai mostly do it on its own?

replies.author: AnyWriting3715
replies.body: Oh no, back then I also had to figure out on my own what each function in the game did. A fair amount of the code I wrote by hand. The architecture I planned myself, and I moved the logic over in pieces rather than by file: map rendering first, then water, then the environment, then the first units, and on from there. Half the optimizations I ended up working out on my own.

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body:
👍👍👍
Hats of for you sir, well done. 

What will you do with it once finished?

replies.author: AnyWriting3715
replies.body: It's been done since January, bugs and all. It'll stay online, and I add to it when I feel like it. The nice part of having the engine ported is that I can put in whatever I want now, so it'll probably keep drifting rather than get a proper 1.0.

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body: Aren't there problems with publishing rights?

replies.author: AnyWriting3715
replies.body: Sure, there are. It's a personal project, not something I'm publishing or making money from, and the assets are the original ones. Making it properly distributable would mean replacing all the art and reworking the mechanics, at which point it isn't a Cossacks port anymore, so there wouldn't be much point.
